title: Gateway state, checkpoints and recovery
summary: Each Gateway owns its execution state independently of the Server. A GatewayRuntimeStateHub holds live jobs, transfers, Docker operation reservations, replay nonces, workers and policies.
html:
Gateway state, checkpoints and recovery

Each Gateway owns its execution state independently of the Server. A GatewayRuntimeStateHub holds live jobs, transfers, Docker operation reservations, replay nonces, workers and policies in RAM. Requests and worker events use that owner; they do not query jobs.db for missing or newer records. The retained GatewayJobs.path property names a legacy import location.

The Server state guide describes a different owner and checkpoint policy. In particular, Gateway RAM limits and its retained previous generation must not be applied to the Server's configuration.

State publication and recovery sequences trace the local owner's bootstrap, transaction conflicts, checkpoint commit point, replay fences, receipt recovery and bounded shutdown branches.

Implementation owners

Owner Responsibility
hub.py Exclusive authority, optimistic transactions, admission indexes, ordered events and shutdown.
files.py Private files, durable JSON publication, root and node leases.
recovery.py Read-only legacy imports, validated restore and complete checkpoint generations.
fences.py Independent dispatch/replay evidence and authenticated completion receipts.
indexes.py and limits.py Conservative resource candidates and explicit resident-state limits.
jobs.py Job registration, admission, authorization, status and reconciliation over the shared hub.
transfer_journal.py Transfer ownership and phase metadata, with durable fences at safety boundaries.
offline commands Inspection, complete safety bundles and explicit previous-generation repair.
flowchart TD A[Acquire root, node and replay leases] --> B[Validate committed generation or initial legacy imports] B --> C[Restore safety fences and signed completion evidence] C --> D[Rebuild indexes and check resident limits] D --> E[READY: live RAM authority] E --> F[Transaction publishes records, indexes and events] F --> E F --> G[Background writer captures immutable roots] G --> H[Write and flush complete generation] H --> I[Publish manifest and acknowledge captured revision] I --> E E --> J[QUIESCING: stop admission and worker IPC] J --> K[Wait for active writer or final checkpoint attempt] K --> L[Release leases when the persistence attempt ends]

Publication and authority

A transaction captures immutable roots and indexes, then computes outside the publication lock. Commit checks that every observed cell and any scanned admission index still match. It publishes records, resource memberships, dirty revisions and sequenced event projections together. A conflict publishes nothing and can retry pure state work. Physical execution, disk writes and process observation must remain outside those retries and the publication lock.

The event deque retains 1,024 recent projections. It is bounded observation history, not a replacement for job state or a durable execution journal. Terminal jobs with uncertain effects can remain in admission indexes until reconciliation establishes what happened. Missing resource classifications produce conservative candidate sets; an index hit alone neither grants permission nor proves a conflict.

Root leases reject a second owner of the same state directory. A separate node lease also rejects a copied root with the same identity on the same machine. Forked children close inherited handles without releasing their parent's lease and cannot reuse its authority. Docker/replay import bindings must be supplied before READY; changing them afterward requires a stopped owner and a complete bootstrap.

Job registration, admission and completion

GatewayJobs uses the shared hub for foreground requests and detached workers. A job ID first names accepted intent: command, cwd, execution settings, resource scope and Controller ownership. Matching repeated start requests return the existing identity's acknowledgement; they do not launch another command. Changed intent cannot reuse the identity to bypass that rule. Passwords are transient launch input, outside the retained job record.

flowchart TD A[Validate intent, runtime and IPC payload] --> B[Reserve identity in READY owner] B --> C{Foreground or detached?} C -->|Foreground| D[Request owns executor stream] C -->|Detached| E[Acquire launch slot and attach worker IPC] E --> F[Wait for physical resource admission] D --> F F --> G[Revalidate authorization and publish dispatch fence] G --> H[Create process and observe execution readiness] H --> I{Authoritative completion receipt?} I -->|Yes| J[Publish process outcome and separate effect facts] I -->|No| K[Retain unknown outcome and reconciliation need]

A detached supervisor process can exist before the target command is admitted. Queued launch work retains the existing identity; cancellation before dispatch can establish that the command did not execute. Once process creation might have occurred, startup failures return uncertainty unless a stronger retained receipt already establishes the result. Private exceptions, command text, environment and settings are excluded from the acknowledgement.

Physical admission compares older conflicting owners and retained uncertain history. Live contention can queue; an unchanged wait eventually becomes an attention result rather than fabricated completion. Stored admission relationships bound blocker inspection, stopping, explicit baseline acceptance and risk grants. Controls compare the owning run, event and relevant revisions before publishing a decision. Stop signals happen after that transaction, outside optimistic retries. An accepted baseline reconciles current effects; it does not rewrite a historical exit code. See resource wait recovery for the Controller-facing workflow.

Status reads retained RAM facts without sampling processes. Explicit inspection samples outside publication and applies diagnostics only when the recorded identity and material state still match, preserving newer worker progress. A visible PID, successful signal or missing process is not a successful task receipt. Likewise, process creation and execution readiness are distinct events; managed temporary-directory preparation can fail between them.

The detached worker selects ordinary, privileged or TTY execution and consumes its completion event. A log-storage failure marks capture unavailable while it keeps consuming that authoritative process stream. Missing completion records an unknown outcome. Output retention, process completion and historical effect reconciliation therefore remain separate facts. Log retention explains byte cursors, eviction and explicit removal.

Public access checks retain the original Controller binding, so pairing a new Controller does not grant it the old owner's jobs. Internal accessors without a request authorization context rely on their service/transport guards. These helpers are not an alternative HTTP authentication boundary.

Recovery and durability

The background writer checks revision lag at two-second intervals or on wakeup. It serializes all domain roots from one snapshot into a fresh private SQLite file and a matching setup record. File checksums, flushes and directory synchronization precede publication of recovery/manifest.json. The manifest selects the committed generation. Newer RAM publications remain dirty after an older snapshot finishes.

The writer retains the current and previous generation. Startup validates the selected manifest, node identity, paths, checksum and SQLite integrity. Once the initialized marker exists, a missing manifest is an error. Corrupt committed state does not trigger an automatic rollback or a return to legacy imports. The SQLite connection/cursor guards permit only explicit bootstrap, checkpoint and repair phases; optional GATEWAY_SQL_AUDIT=1 also checks process-level opens.

Checkpoints can lag live state. Separate private safety records cover facts that must survive that lag: dispatch reservations, consumed nonces, transfer ownership, Docker operation reservations and verified terminal receipts. A dispatch fence without completion evidence restores an unknown job requiring reconciliation. It does not permit another dispatch. Receipts must match their intent, identity and signature before they can resolve an uncertain outcome. Log-retirement records prevent a restored checkpoint from resurrecting purged output.

Diagnostics distinguish checkpointed, dirty and degraded persistence and report RAM/committed revisions, dirty age and bytes, failure count and checkpoint duration. A successful status read does not imply its latest facts are checkpointed. Shutdown stops admission and IPC, then waits for the active writer and, when applicable, a final checkpoint attempt. A late writer retains owner leases until it finishes; a timeout does not authorize an overlapping replacement. hub.close() reports shutdown completion, not checkpoint success. Its final-write branch releases leases even when that attempt fails; its late-background-writer branch joins the old writer without starting another final snapshot. See the shutdown sequence before interpreting this return value as a durable drain.

Startup validation and connection output

Runtime readiness checks local execution imports, the supported psutil range (5.9 through versions below 8.0) and process-identity support. Successful results are cached. The runtime revision hashes sorted top-level gateway_core/*.py filenames and contents, plus the compiled build ID when present; it is a build/source observation, not a health lease or execution grant. Source comments also contribute to that content hash. Capabilities add the current purge epoch separately instead of caching it here.

The production readiness command also verifies that aor-runtime is installed without editable metadata or a mismatched source overlay, and requires HTTP dependencies to be ready. Core validation used by other callers can succeed when the optional HTTP provider is unavailable. Failure returns a common installer remediation message; this module installs nothing and makes no network probe.

Startup output prints the effective node, listener addresses or outbound Server URL and optional public-key fingerprint. Its shared formatter discovers local interfaces for wildcard listeners. These registration hints do not establish remote reachability or completed pairing.

Runtime purge and pairing reset

The operator workflow is authoritative for confirmation, UI progress and offline commands. Runtime purge is a separate maintenance operation from local connection reset.

Operation Changes Retained state
Runtime purge Disposable job/transfer/Docker/worker history, owned output caches, managed browser execution history and eligible logs Policies, nonces/replay protection, TLS/controller identity, configuration and reusable account setup
Connection reset Controller enrollment, hashed cached Server-peer records and abandoned identity temporary files TLS identity, replay protection, job history, artifacts, configuration and unrelated files

The closed inventory classifies every recovery domain and recognized runtime-root child. New unclassified collections fail validation. The filesystem plan rejects unknown managed artifact/scratch/log entries, linked or shared files, unexpected mounts, mixed-node legacy Docker records and shared managed storage with another instance's ownership evidence. Node-specific local-AI state is selected separately from installed runtimes and model downloads. A ready preview estimates eligible bytes; it does not prove that writers have stopped, and an unavailable size remains unknown.

Browser selection removes whole session-prefixed profile trees. Reusable profiles need an application ownership marker and retain account/setup files while known history, session, cache and log paths are selected. Preview tolerates active singleton markers, but deletion planning refuses a profile with a remaining SingletonLock.

A paired-controller prepare request creates the operation journal and moves the hub to QUIESCING. Ordinary requests then fail admission; fixed management paths remain available. purge starts a drain/restart thread. It seals worker launch, stops verified descendant identities, waits for counted requests, closes artifact/browser/transfer/mail writers and flushes the final checkpoint. Failure records a blocked operation and permits an explicit retry; it does not return a successful purge receipt while writers remain unresolved.

flowchart LR A[Prepare journal and quiesce] --> B[Drain writers and request replacement] B --> C[Exclusive offline recovery] C --> D[Preserve setup and preflight inventory] D --> E[Publish epoch and remove disposable state] E --> F[Write and verify fresh generation] F --> G[Await controller release] G --> H[Accept requests with the new signed epoch]

Recovery runs before restoring the job hub. Root, node, lifecycle and replay leases protect the offline operation. Before deletion it saves policy/nonce data independently, binds the storage roots in the journal and checks the full filesystem inventory. It publishes the new epoch before deleting ownership history, cleans identity-bound transfer stages and writes a flushed recovery generation containing retained collections. Restore verification must find the disposable collections empty. Once prepared, interrupted work resumes from its saved setup and moves forward; changing the bound storage roots blocks it.

Current checkpoints supply a checksummed independent setup file, allowing recovery even when disposable database payloads are corrupt. Older checkpoints require readable preserved collections. Damaged replay records are removed only after holding exclusive authentication ownership for a full nonce lifetime; interruption starts a new full wait. Corrupt or missing preserved setup cannot become defaults.

A local purge completes after verification. A remotely initiated purge remains awaiting_release until its paired Controller releases that same verified operation. Requests from the previous signed epoch remain stale afterward. Repeated matching status/prepare/purge requests do not create another operation or repeat already verified deletion. The offline CLI requires the exact confirmation phrase; even its preview acquires the exclusive lifecycle lease.

Connection reset has a smaller scope. Its dry run validates the cleanup plan without creating state. Mutation acquires lifecycle and identity locks, revalidates the paths, writes a new unpaired enrollment revision and deletes only selected peer/temporary files. It keeps the replay ledger so rapidly pairing the same Controller again cannot authorize replay of an old signed request. Stop the selected Gateway before reset and use its original instance/TLS-state selectors.

Local software-update admission

GatewayUpdater owns the local execution fence and installation journal for an authenticated update command. Controller Gateway routes handle registry management and owner-selected releases; the controller coordinator first cancels affected tasks and sends checkpointed intent. The local updater then checks the exact descriptor, protocol, expected installed build and registered live installation. Its journal records the package-bound authorization before the start response is acknowledged.

Operation IDs bind the descriptor and expected old build. Replaying a matching receipt returns that result; changing its package conflicts. A cancellation arriving before start creates a retained cancelled receipt, so a delayed start cannot install anything. Existing active operations, failed rollback and pending runtime purge prevent a different update from being accepted.

The shared admission lock in runtime_purge.admit serializes request registration with update acceptance. It calls the updater's guard, increments counted requests and decrements them in finally. New execution is held while an update is active. Observation, cancellation, model-stop controls and allowed existing transfer cleanup operations remain available through their usual authorization and validation. These exceptions let callers resolve blockers without opening another execution path.

Local blocker Required observation
Admitted requests Their request contexts have exited
Jobs The runtime hub has no active job owners
Transfers Existing transfer sessions have closed
POSIX terminals Open terminal sessions have closed; this blocker scan is POSIX-specific
Gateway-managed models Neither the local-AI owner nor the legacy model process remains live

The updater cancels these owners after accepting the durable operation. While waiting_for_idle, its monitor reports stopping progress. Cleanup shares a two-second grace period, followed by identity-checked termination and up to five seconds to verify exit. Only owned process trees are eligible; updater helpers and unrelated processes are excluded. Unconfirmed cleanup becomes stop_failed with an explicit retry, while cancellation history and uncertain effects stay retained. updater.stops_work advertises this additive behavior without changing package compatibility.

When that helper marks restarting, the old build writes a checkpoint and verifies that its committed revision covers the observed hub revision before publishing drained. The Gateway helper waits up to 30 seconds for that receipt before its normal replacement step; the Server's separate final-save protocol has different waiting behavior. See independent replacement and readiness.

Returning Gateway processes publish their own build/boot/process receipt. Local health exposes only minimal build/boot identity for the update probe; it does not replace the controller's authenticated readiness check. verifying_connection remains held until the controller confirms the expected build and ready runtime. Helper startup failures before activation become failed; failures during activation become rollback_failed, which keeps execution fenced for recovery. Terminal receipts survive late status/cancel requests rather than replaying effects.

Signed transport tests cover durable acknowledgement, altered requests, cancellation overtaking start and shared HTTP/outbound handling with installation effects isolated. The operator guide describes release selection, local blockers, journal diagnostics and qualification limits.

Transfer stage ownership and cleanup

TransferJournal uses the shared RAM hub with node/run/transfer keys and a hub-level lock shared by independently constructed providers. It stores metadata, not file bytes. Stage creation records the exact file and parent device/inode/owner identities in a safety fence before acknowledging bytes. At 256 retained records, admission can evict only the oldest cleaned terminal record; otherwise it rejects capacity.

A committing fence must succeed before commit intent is published. If a later terminal fence fails, current RAM truth is retained with degraded persistence; the earlier intent still prevents automatic replay. Checkpoint durability remains separate from acknowledging byte progress.

Cleanup considers at most 32 oldest eligible records per pass, skips live sessions, and applies the protocol idle threshold. It unlinks only the exact registered hidden-stage name under the original pinned parent. Replaced files, unexpected links and special files are refused. The two-link no-clobber publication window is allowed only when stage and visible destination identify the same owned inode; cleanup preserves the destination. There is no recursive search for matching filenames.

Completed cleanup retains metadata for reconciliation until its 24-hour retention threshold. Uncertain/committing states are not converted into successful outcomes. Cleanup errors update the record to rotate it behind other eligible work; an unavailable journal can still fail the pass. Provider shutdown must precede hub closure so background expiry does not attempt to read an owner that has closed.

Detached workers and retained output

The internal worker protocol connects independent supervisors to the RAM owner with protected tickets, authenticated loopback frames and exact process/socket identity. A successful attachment is not an execution grant. Resource admission and the durable dispatch fence precede a fresh grant; reconnecting a worker does not recreate its command.

Worker event acknowledgements confirm RAM acceptance. Signed terminal receipts and checkpoints provide separate durability evidence. Terminal-input delivery has its own identified acknowledgement; a lost reply remains unknown and does not authorize replay. Session loss and a failed control read likewise do not establish that an external process stopped.

Job output uses a separate bounded FIFO segment store with absolute cursors. Expired cursors return explicit eviction/continuation information. Retirement is recorded before physical chunk deletion, preserving the fence if deletion fails or a writer finishes late. Compact progress previews describe actual output and retain producer timestamps; observing a job never manufactures progress. The protocol guide is the authoritative description of these output and delivery limits.

Gateway RAM limits

These settings belong to the Gateway process and are read when its hub is created. They measure serialized record bytes, not total process RSS.

Variable Default Minimum
GATEWAY_RAM_MAX_JOBS 120,000 1
GATEWAY_RAM_MAX_ACTIVE 1,000 1
GATEWAY_RAM_MAX_RECORD_BYTES 1,048,576 65,536
GATEWAY_RAM_MAX_BYTES 1,073,741,824 1,048,576

Malformed or undersized settings fail configuration. Record-size and admission checks reject excessive growth; they do not evict uncertain jobs or read through to SQL. Terminal/control updates can reduce pressure. Restored state exceeding the record, total-byte or job-count budget fails startup and requires an explicit offline configuration adjustment.

Offline inspection and safety bundles

For a source checkout, the command surface is:

PYTHONPATH=src .venv/bin/python -m gateway_core.runtime_state inspect /path/to/gateway-jobs
PYTHONPATH=src .venv/bin/python -m gateway_core.runtime_state validate /path/to/gateway-jobs
PYTHONPATH=src .venv/bin/python -m gateway_core.runtime_state backup /path/to/gateway-jobs --destination /path/to/new-bundle
PYTHONPATH=src .venv/bin/python -m gateway_core.runtime_state restore /path/to/new-bundle --destination /path/to/new-installation-state

inspect and validate perform the same validation and print identity, revision and domain counts. Existing-owner operations acquire root, node and replay leases; stop that Gateway before using them. Backup also requires every recorded worker to be definitively drained. Unknown process liveness blocks it. The destination must be new, and its parent must already exist.

A backup includes the Gateway tree and bound TLS/replay state, plus a configured legacy Docker import when present. Restore creates a new destination and returns gateway_root and, when applicable, tls_root. Configure the restored installation with those matching roots. Treat the bundle as private: it contains identity and authentication material. Copying only a checkpoint database omits independent safety evidence and is not a complete backup.

When a current generation is corrupt, the explicit previous action can validate the previous generation and every independent safety fence, require drained workers, save the old manifest bytes in pre-repair.json and select the previous manifest. It changes recovery state and must be a deliberate operator repair. It does not discard dispatch fences or turn uncertain effects into completed work.

Regression evidence

RAM state tests cover detached reads, transaction conflicts, import preservation, SQL guards, nonce replay and owner isolation. Fault tests exercise manifest crash boundaries, newer dirty revisions, failed fence writes and signed completion evidence. Operation tests cover complete bundles, previous-generation repair, capacity, event order and surviving-worker refusal. These isolated fixtures do not certify every native OS ACL, filesystem or production recovery environment.
